name: Thomas Paine
role: English-American pamphleteer of the American and French Revolutions (1737–1809)
summary: Thomas Paine, author of Common Sense, The Rights of Man and The Age of Reason, argued for American independence, republican government without hereditary rule, universal male suffrage, a national fund for every citizen funded by a ground-rent on land, and a deist rejection of revealed churches.

booksNotUsed.reason: A second Project Gutenberg edition of Common Sense; the 147 text is the one read and cited.

booksNotUsed.file: 3741 Paine - The Writings of Thomas Paine — Volume 1 (1774-1779) The Ame.txt
booksNotUsed.reason: The American Crisis (vol. 1, 1774-79): wartime pamphlets read by theme (slavery, war, army); the only slavery passage uses 'slavery' for Britain's claim to bind the colonies, and the pamphlets state no position on the test's statements beyond independence, already cited from Common Sense.

booksNotUsed.file: 15279 Paine - A Letter Addressed to the Abbe Raynal, on the Affairs of Nor.txt
booksNotUsed.reason: Letter to the Abbe Raynal on the affairs of North America (1782), read by theme (taxation, religion, slavery, monarchy): a defence of the American cause with no new position.

booksNotUsed.file: 31270 Paine - The Writings of Thomas Paine, Complete With Index to Volumes.txt
booksNotUsed.reason: The complete Writings with index: the same volumes cited above (vols. 2 and 3) and the American Crisis, Age of Reason volumes read separately.

booksNotUsed.file: 69464 Paine - Light from the spirit world The pilgrimage of Thomas Paine a.txt
booksNotUsed.reason: A spiritualist book of 'communications' attributed to Paine's spirit: not by Paine, so no evidence of his positions.

notes: First audit, from his four main works read by theme in the Gutenberg texts (the editor's introductions by Moncure Conway were not counted as his words). Agrarian Justice is the source for the inheritance, ground-rent and basic-income answers; the proposal is a lump sum at 21 and an annuity from 50, so the basic-income answer is medium. The 1793 speech 'Reasons for Preserving the Life of Louis Capet' (in vol. 3) is cited for the death penalty. Searched without a settled answer: slavery as an institution (the volumes read hold only his use of 'slavery' for colonial subjection), war and standing armies, and free trade. Most statements stay null.
